title: The Kestrel Line
subtitle: Vienna, Berlin, Istanbul: Fourteen Days in the Autumn of 1983

listing.title: The Kestrel Line 🕵️
listing.blurb: November 1983: a KGB colonel wants out, your own station has a mole, and NATO is days from rehearsing a nuclear war that Moscow half believes is real. Run the defector from Vienna through the Wall to Istanbul and back with payphones, dead drops and nerve, because every gunshot is a headline. Levels 3–8.

synopsis: Autumn 1983 is the most dangerous season of the Cold War that almost nobody noticed. Soviet air defence has shot down a Korean airliner, Pershing II missiles are about to arrive in West Germany, and in Moscow an ageing, frightened leadership has spent two years ordering its spies to find the signs of a Western nuclear first strike, a standing order called RYAN, and its spies, being human, have found them. In the first week of November, NATO will run a command-post exercise that rehearses the release of nuclear weapons, with new codes and new procedures, and in Moscow there are men who believe it may not be an exercise at all. The party are a team of the Annex, a small, deniable Anglo-American intelligence cell run out of a shipping-insurance office in Vienna. On 28 October a chalk mark appears on a lamppost by the Naschmarkt and a note appears in a dead drop the Annex thought was secret. It is from a KGB colonel, codename KESTREL, who wants out, and she is offering two things: the RYAN file, which proves Moscow is genuinely afraid, and the name of the mole inside the Annex's own Vienna station. Over fourteen days the party must meet her under the noses of Czech watchers in Vienna, bring her out of East Berlin through the transit autobahn in a car with a hidden compartment, chase her insurance copy of the microfilm across a martial-law Istanbul on the eve of an election, and come home to Vienna to unmask and deal with the mole before he sends the one report that could turn an exercise into a catastrophe. The opposition is professional and the guns are real, but every shot is heard for blocks and every body is a headline, and the campaign rewards dry-cleaning, cover stories and patience far above marksmanship. History says the world did not end in November 1983. This campaign is about the people who made sure.
hook: Vienna, Friday 28 October 1983, a little after seven in the morning. It is raining on the Linke Wienzeile and the Naschmarkt traders are still putting out the crates. On the third lamppost from the corner of the Kettenbruckengasse, at knee height, someone has drawn a small horizontal chalk line with a short tick at its right end, which in the Annex's signal book means DOVECOTE IS LOADED and has not been used since 1979, because DOVECOTE is a dead drop in the Hofbauer family vault at the Zentralfriedhof and only five people alive are supposed to know it exists. By eleven the team is standing in the wet among the graves of strangers. Inside the vault door, wrapped in a plastic bread bag, is a single sheet from a Soviet one-time pad with a message in plain Russian on the back: I am a colonel of the First Chief Directorate. I wish to come over. I will bring the RYAN file. I will give you the name of your gardener. Signal acceptance by Monday. And under it, to prove she is real, the true name of an agent the Annex lost in Budapest in 1977, which has never been written down anywhere on this side of the Iron Curtain.

setting.name: Central Europe and the Bosphorus, 28 October to 11 November 1983
setting.description: The real Europe of late 1983, with fictional people moving through it. Vienna is the neutral capital of the spy trade: café tables, the UN agencies, the Ringstrasse trams, and more intelligence officers per square mile than anywhere on earth, all watching each other. Berlin is two cities with a concrete wall between them: West Berlin an island of punks, draft dodgers and Allied soldiers, East Berlin a capital of grey façades, Trabants and the Stasi, joined by checkpoints and by transit autobahns where Western cars may drive through the GDR but may not stop. Istanbul is three years into military rule after the 1980 coup, under martial law, with soldiers on the bridges and a general election on Sunday 6 November, and it has always been the place where the routes from the Balkans arrive. Nobody carries a telephone. Messages travel by payphone and code phrase, by telex from an office with a cipher machine, by one-time pad and numbers station, by chalk mark, by thumbtack, by a cassette left under a bench. Film has to be developed. Passports have to be stamped. A car crossing the Wall takes forty minutes if nobody is interested in it and eight hours if somebody is. The party works for the Annex, a fictional joint cell of British and American officers set up in 1979 to run the operations neither government would put its name to, out of the third floor of Danubia Marine Assurance on the Schwarzenbergplatz. The opposition are the real services of the period, staffed in this campaign entirely by fictional people: the KGB's Vienna residency and its Berlin headquarters at Karlshorst, the East German Ministry for State Security, the Czechoslovak StB watchers who do much of the KGB's legwork in Vienna, the Bulgarian DS, and Turkey's MIT, who are on nobody's side but Turkey's.
setting.atmosphere: Cigarette smoke, wet cobbles, sodium streetlight, the hiss of a payphone line before the pips. Tension, not action: the long minutes in a café pretending to read Die Presse while a man in a green loden coat pretends to read his; the moment at a checkpoint when the guard looks at a passport photograph for one second too long. This is le Carré, not Bond. Violence is rare, ugly and loud, and it has consequences that outlast the scene: police, newspapers, a blown legend, a burned safe-house, a station that can no longer protect you. Competence is the fantasy here. Let the players feel clever when they spot a tail, choose a meeting place with three exits, or turn an enemy with a conversation instead of a bullet. Ground every scene in period detail: Walkmans and Telefunken radios, ashtrays everywhere, Deutschmarks and schillings, West Berlin punk and East Berlin Schlager, cassette tapes, Polaroids, telex paper curling out of a machine at three in the morning. No internet, no mobile phones, no satellite pictures on demand. Information is slow, physical and stealable.

regions.name: Vienna
regions.description: The neutral city at the hinge of East and West, and the campaign's home. The Ringstrasse and its trams; the Naschmarkt and the Linke Wienzeile; the Riesenrad in the Prater, whose slow gondolas are the best twelve-minute private room in Europe; the vast Zentralfriedhof where the Annex keeps its oldest dead drop; the Café Landtmann where diplomats are overheard on purpose. The Annex station is on the Schwarzenbergplatz, a few hundred metres from the Soviet war memorial. The KGB residency works out of the Soviet embassy in the Reisnerstrasse and the mission to the international organisations; Czech StB watchers do its street work. Austrian State Police tolerate everyone as long as nobody shoots. Somebody is about to shoot.

regions.name: Berlin, West and East
regions.description: West Berlin: Tegel airport (only Allied airlines may fly in), Kreuzberg's squats and Turkish grocers, the Wall's graffiti, Checkpoint Charlie and its American MPs, the transit autobahn south through Dreilinden toward Helmstedt and the West. East Berlin: the Friedrichstrasse border station that Berliners call the Palace of Tears, the mandatory exchange of 25 Deutschmarks, the TV tower over Alexanderplatz, the Hotel Stadt Berlin full of Western businessmen and the men who watch them, and in Karlshorst the walled compound of the KGB's largest station outside the Soviet Union. Under the city, West Berlin's U-Bahn trains still run through sealed 'ghost stations' beneath the East, where Transport Police stand on dim platforms and watch the trains go by without stopping.

regions.name: Istanbul
regions.description: A city of six million under martial law three years after the coup, with army checkpoints on the Galata and Ataturk bridges, a midnight curfew in some districts, and election posters for three permitted parties on every wall ahead of polling day on 6 November. Sirkeci station, where the Orient Express used to arrive; the Pudding Shop in Sultanahmet, still a noticeboard for the hippie trail; the Grand Bazaar's labyrinth; the TIR truck parks of Laleli and Aksaray where the trucks from Bulgaria and Yugoslavia arrive; the hamams; the ferries criss-crossing the Bosphorus to Kadikoy and Uskudar; and the old wooden yalis along the European shore where a launch can tie up after dark.

regions.name: The Vienna Woods
regions.description: The wooded hills on Vienna's western edge: vineyards, Heurigen wine taverns, the Kahlenberg and Leopoldsberg looking down on the Danube, and on a forestry track above Weidling an old hunting lodge the Annex uses as its deep safe-house and radio relay, with a long-wire antenna in the trees and a teleprinter in the cellar. It is where KESTREL is held in the endgame, and where the last night of the exercise is waited out.

campaignRules.name: Heat
campaignRules.description: The party has a single Heat score per city, 0 to 10, which the GM tracks openly in the world state. Heat measures how much attention the opposition and the local police are paying to the team. It rises: +1 for each failed surveillance-detection run or blown brush pass; +1 for using a true name or a burned legend; +2 for a body found; +2 for a gunshot wound treated in a hospital (they report them); +3 for each exchange of unsuppressed gunfire in a city (suppressed: +1); +3 for a car chase that the police see. It falls by 1 for each full day the team spends quiet (no operations, no meetings), and resets to 2 when the team enters a new city under fresh legends. Thresholds: Heat 3, the local service assigns a watcher team (surveillance becomes the default, not the exception); Heat 6, the local service actively hunts the team, borders and airports have their legends, the police will stop them on sight; Heat 9, the Annex disowns them in that city: safe-houses close, money stops, and any arrest is their own problem. Heat is the campaign's real hit-point track. Tell players their Heat every time it changes.

campaignRules.name: Legends (Cover Identities)
campaignRules.description: Each character carries a cover passport and a legend, a cover life with a job, an address and people who will vouch for it. Each legend sheet line states its strength (thin, good, excellent). A legend is challenged whenever an official, a border guard or a suspicious contact pushes on it: a Deception check, DC 12 for a casual question, DC 15 for a border or police interview, DC 18 for a professional counter-intelligence interrogation. Thin legends roll with disadvantage when anyone checks by telephone or visit; excellent legends roll with advantage. A failure by less than 5 earns suspicion (+1 Heat); a failure by 5 or more blows the legend permanently. A blown legend cannot be used again anywhere in the campaign. Augustin Moser can build a replacement passport in 24 hours, but a passport is not a legend: a new one is always thin.

campaignRules.name: Tradecraft: Dry Cleaning
campaignRules.description: Before any meet, drop or safe-house visit, the team may run a surveillance-detection route (SDR): one to two hours on foot and by public transport, doubling back, using shop windows and tram stops. Make a group Streetwise check (Perception may substitute for one character on overwatch) against the opposition's DC: Austrian police 10, Czech StB watchers in Vienna 14, KGB Line KR 15, Stasi in East Berlin 17, MIT in Istanbul 15. Success: the team knows whether it is followed and can choose to lose the tail (a second check) or abort. Failure: the team believes it is clean. Failure by 5 or more: it is followed and the opposition knows it has been spotted trying. Skipping the SDR is allowed and frequently fatal. A clean SDR before a meeting should be the most satisfying thing in the session; play it as a scene, not a roll.

campaignRules.name: Dead Drops, Signals and Brush Passes
campaignRules.description: Agents rarely meet. They leave things. A signal site (a chalk mark, a thumbtack in a noticeboard, a parked car with its window down an inch) says a drop is loaded or a meeting is on. A dead drop (a loose brick, a hollow bolt, a vault door, a magnetic box under a bench) holds film, cash or messages. A brush pass hands something over in a second as two people cross. Loading or emptying a drop unobserved is a Sleight of Hand or Stealth check, DC 13, or DC 17 if the team is under surveillance. A brush pass is two checks, one by each party, DC 14; if either fails, a watcher may see it. Every drop has a tell (a matchstick, a fold, a hair across a seam) that shows whether it has been opened by someone else; Perception or Investigation DC 13 notices a disturbed tell. Disturbed tells are clues, and the GM should plant them honestly.

campaignRules.name: Comms: No Phones, No Network
campaignRules.description: There are no mobile telephones and no internet. To reach the station the team uses a payphone and a clear-code phrase ('Is that the Danube shipping office? I am calling about the Linz consignment') and costs one coin and a minute on an exchange anyone might tap. Hotel phones are tapped in East Berlin as a matter of course and in Istanbul often. Long messages go by telex from the station or a friendly business, enciphered on a one-time pad (30 minutes to encipher or decipher a page; a captured pad compromises every message on it). Film must be developed (Gus Moser, 2 hours) and read on a microfilm reader. IMPORTANT FOR THE GM: until the mole is unmasked, every message the team sends to or through the Vienna station is read by GARDENER and reaches the KGB within 6 to 24 hours. Track what GARDENER knows in the world state. The opposition should act on exactly that knowledge, no more, so that players who stop using the station see the leaks stop, which is the best clue in the campaign.

campaignRules.name: Loud Is Lethal
campaignRules.description: The core gunplay rules apply in full and are deliberately harsh. On top of them: a gunshot in a city brings police, in about 3 minutes in Vienna or West Berlin, in under 1 minute in East Berlin (Volkspolizei, Transport Police and Stasi are everywhere), and in 1d6 minutes in Istanbul, where it will be soldiers. Gunfire adds Heat as above. A wounded character cannot go to a hospital without +2 Heat and a police report; Dr. Brandt, a bent vet in Ottakring, or a back-room doctor Selim knows are the alternatives. Bodies must be explained or hidden. Opposition professionals know all of this too: a KGB or Stasi team would rather snatch than shoot, and will usually break contact if a fight goes loud. Reward the party for avoiding fights: a meeting held without anyone drawing a weapon is worth story XP equal to a won fight.

campaignRules.name: The Calendar
campaignRules.description: The campaign runs on a fixed calendar and the GM tracks the date and hour in the world state. Fixed events happen whether or not the party is ready: Mon 31 Oct, KESTREL flies to East Berlin on recall. Thu 3 Nov, KESTREL is due to be put on an Aeroflot flight to Moscow from Schonefeld, after which she is beyond reach. Sat 5 Nov, the Bulgarian courier's truck reaches Istanbul. Sun 6 Nov, Turkish general election, extra troops on the streets. Mon 7 Nov, the NATO exercise begins. Night of Wed 9 to Thu 10 Nov, the exercise rehearses nuclear release, and GARDENER has an emergency transmission scheduled to Moscow for 02:00. Fri 11 Nov, the exercise ends. Each day has about six useful scenes of time; travel between cities costs most of a day (Vienna to West Berlin by Pan Am via Frankfurt, Vienna to Istanbul by Turkish Airlines or the overnight train). Time is a resource the party spends, and it should feel scarce.

campaignRules.name: Money and Local Cash
campaignRules.description: All money is tracked in dollars in each character's wallet line, as the campaign's working currency. Schillings, Deutschmarks, East marks and Turkish lira exist in the fiction; convert them at the time of spending. Rough 1983 prices: a café and cake $3, a Vienna tram ticket $1, a payphone call 25 cents, a cheap hotel $25 a night, a good one $120, a rented car $40 a day, a bribe to a petty official $20 to $100, a used car for cash $1,500, a forged passport from someone who is not Gus $800. The East German compulsory day-visa exchange is 25 DM, about $10. The team's operational float is carried by Julian Ashcombe; the station replenishes it until the team stops trusting the station.

explorationRules: This is a city campaign and the map is a schematic of Europe: four operational theatres joined by aeroplanes, trains and one very long autobahn. Travel between cities takes most of a day and should be narrated briskly but never skipped, because borders are where legends are tested: every airport and frontier is a Legends check, and the GM should make at least one of them tense in each scenario. Within a city, the party moves by tram, U-Bahn, taxi, ferry and on foot, and the unit of time is the scene (roughly two hours). Run each city as a small sandbox of named places (each scenario lists them) with the opposition acting on its own clock and on what it knows. The opposition is not omniscient: it knows what GARDENER has passed on, what its watchers have seen, and what the party's Heat implies. Narrate surveillance concretely and fairly: the same green loden coat twice, a Skoda with Vienna plates and a man reading a newspaper in it, a woman who gets off the tram one stop after you and on again one stop later. Skill checks are stated with a DC and a failure outcome; failures cost time, Heat or position, and almost never end the operation outright. Every important clue has at least two routes to it. Between scenes, let the cities breathe: the smell of the Naschmarkt, a punk band in a Kreuzberg cellar, the call to prayer over the Golden Horn at dawn, a radio news bulletin about Pershing missiles and peace marches. The players should come away knowing what autumn 1983 felt like.

controlFile.note: The fixed truth of the campaign, for the GM only. Like a character's hit points, this does not change because a player has a more exciting theory. All characters are fictional; the historical backdrop (Operation RYAN, the November 1983 NATO exercise, the Wall, martial law in Turkey, the 6 November Turkish election) is real. No real living person appears or is depicted. Heads of state and real officials stay off-stage and unnamed.
controlFile.theMole: GARDENER is Lionel Pryce, 44, the Annex Vienna station's communications officer, who runs the telex room, holds the one-time pads, keeps the station's safe-house list, and reads every message in and out. Recruited in Nicosia in 1971 by Vera Tarasova (KESTREL) herself, through gambling debts and a sick mother, posted as comms clerk to the British embassy in Budapest from 1976 to 1978, where his reporting betrayed the Annex agent HEMLOCK (Gabor) in 1977, the loss Martin Vell blames himself for and the name KESTREL used as her bona fides; and run since 1979, when he joined the Annex, by the KGB Vienna residency's Line KR officer, Yuri Golovkin. He passes copies of station traffic by dead drop (a loose stone in the wall of the Steinhof church grounds) and, in emergency, by a burst transmitter hidden in a Grundig radio in his flat in Dobling. He is not a monster. He is a frightened, lonely, clever man who has been trapped for twelve years and has come to believe, like the people reading his reports, that the West may really be planning a first strike, because he has been asked to look for signs of one so often. In the last three weeks his reports on the coming exercise have been increasingly alarmed and partly embellished. Moscow has asked him to send an immediate report at 02:00 on the night of 9/10 November, during the exercise's nuclear-release phase, on whether the Annex and its American partners believe the release is real. That report matters.
redHerrings: Martin Vell, 56, station chief: drinks, has a Hungarian girlfriend (Ilona, a pianist, entirely innocent), has gambling losses at the Casino Baden, and has been unusually reluctant to take KESTREL seriously. He is loyal, tired, and ashamed. His reluctance is because he lost the Budapest agent in 1977 and has never forgiven himself; KESTREL's bona fides open that wound.

Hal Brennan, 41, a CIA officer from the US embassy in Vienna who wants KESTREL for himself and has been sniffing around the Annex. He is a rival, not a traitor: he has a source of his own inside the station (Vell's secretary, who gossips), which explains some leaks and muddies the water.
Augustin Moser's StB forgery in 1979, which the opposition can use against him, and which looks like treachery if it surfaces before the party understands it.
clues: M1: The DOVECOTE tell (a matchstick in the vault door hinge) was replaced on the left; every Annex officer is trained to set it on the right, and Pryce, left-handed, services DOVECOTE on the station's quarterly schedule. (cw-scenario-001)
M2: The Gumpendorfer Strasse safe-house is hit within hours of the team telexing its use; only Vell, Pryce and the Controller in London had the address. (cw-scenario-001)

M3: The station's outbound telex counter runs higher than Pryce's log, by the length of a short message, on the nights before two blown operations this year. Dee Coleman has noticed and dismissed it. (cw-scenario-001 or 004)

M4: Rybak's team knows the transit-route car's colour and plates in Berlin, which the team telexed to Vienna for the station to clear with the Allied liaison; they do not know the rest-stop, which the team did not send. (cw-scenario-002)

M5: The Istanbul microfilm contains KESTREL's 1971 Nicosia recruitment report, naming a British signals clerk, L. P., left-handed, with a sick mother in Croydon; and three weeks of GARDENER's recent reports on the exercise. (cw-scenario-003)
M6: The canary trap: three versions of a fake message, one each to Vell, Pryce and Brennan, and only Pryce's version provokes a response at the KGB residency. (cw-scenario-004)
M7: Augustin Moser's 1982 microfilm duplicate of a station log sheet in Pryce's handwriting, showing a message number skipped. (cw-scenario-004)

M8: Two missing morphine syrettes from the safe-house kit; Pryce restocked it and took them for his mother, who died in a Croydon hospice three weeks ago, and has kept them in his desk since, as he keeps everything. Petty, sad, and a confirmation of character rather than of treachery.
controlFile.kestrelsTerms: Vera Tarasova will give GARDENER's name only on Western soil and in exchange for a written guarantee of resettlement in North America from someone above the Vienna station. A party that wins her trust (Insight or Persuasion DC 20 after a shared danger, or simply by keeping every promise they make her) can get it from her earlier. If the party learns the name before cw-scenario-004, that scenario becomes about proving it, keeping Pryce from bolting, and deciding what to do with him; it should not be skipped.
controlFile.outcomes: History is not changed. The November 1983 exercise ended on 11 November without war, and the campaign keeps it that way: failure is personal, not apocalyptic. If the party fails (Pryce sends his alarmed report, KESTREL dies, the film is lost), Moscow spends a frightening 36 hours at higher readiness, aircraft are fuelled on East German runways, nothing happens, and the party carries the knowledge of how close it was; the Annex is shut down in the spring of 1984. If the party succeeds (Pryce is turned and sends a calm report, or is stopped and the RYAN film reaches someone with the authority to quietly tone down the exercise), the last night passes with Moscow reassured, and the party's evidence becomes one small reason the West begins, in 1984, to change its tone. Either way the world does not end. The difference is who the party are when it does not.
